title: Service control policies: guardrails inherited down the tree

videos.script: An administrator of an account can do anything in it. That is what administrator means. {{admin}} So how does a company stop an administrator from switching off its logs, or starting machines on another continent? {{question}} With a rule that sits above the account, where its administrators cannot reach. That rule is a service control policy. {{scp}} It never grants anything. It sets a ceiling, and every request in the account has to fit under it. IAM decides what a role may do. The policies above decide the most that anyone there may do. {{ceiling}} The ceilings stack down the tree. A request has to be allowed at every level, from the root to the account, and denied at none. {{tree}} In this lesson you write four of them for the shop. Nobody leaves the organisation. Nothing runs outside São Paulo. Nobody switches off the logs. And nobody but the platform changes the deployer. {{four}} Then you watch moto ignore all four. It stores the policies and decides nothing with them. So what AWS would refuse comes from AWS's documentation, and the lab shows you only the shape. {{end}}
